quiz.why: Oscillometric cuffs are unreliable in irregular rhythms, so manual verification comes first. Charting an artifact mislabels the patient, picking the higher of two machine readings is not a method, and delaying 15 minutes risks missing real hypotension.

quiz.q: A blood pressure cuff that is too small for a patient's arm will produce what error?
choices: A falsely low reading
A falsely high reading
No reading at all
An accurate reading with a wider pulse pressure
quiz.why: An undersized bladder requires more pressure to compress the artery, so the measured value reads falsely high. An oversized cuff has the opposite effect and reads falsely low, which is how real hypertension gets missed.

quiz.q: A 4-year-old needs medication dosing. His mother says he weighs 'about 40 pounds.' What should you do?
choices: Enter 40 in the weight field and note it is an estimate
Convert 40 pounds to kilograms mentally and enter that
Weigh the child on a scale in kilograms, or use a length-based tape if he cannot be weighed
Use the average weight for a 4-year-old
quiz.why: Every pediatric dose, bolus, and energy setting is per kilogram, so the weight is a calculation input and must be measured, not recalled. Parental estimates and age averages both introduce dosing error, and mental conversions invite unit mistakes.

quiz.q: Why is the respiratory rate considered a high-value vital sign in triage?
choices: It is the easiest to measure accurately
It correlates directly with blood pressure
It is required for billing
It is one of the earliest measurable signs of deterioration, and it is also the most frequently falsified
quiz.why: Respiratory rate rises early in sepsis, shock, and respiratory failure, often before blood pressure changes. It is also the vital sign most often charted without being counted, which destroys its predictive value.

quiz.q: An ESI 3 patient has been in the waiting room for 50 minutes. His initial heart rate was 104. What should have happened by now?
choices: A full set of repeat vitals, since ESI 3 patients are rechecked every 30 to 60 minutes and his initial rate was abnormal
Nothing; the level was already assigned
A recheck only if he approaches the desk
Automatic upgrade to ESI 2 based on wait time
quiz.why: Reassessment is the safety net under a triage level, and an initially abnormal heart rate makes him a priority for rechecks. Wait time alone does not change acuity, and relying on the patient to report a change misses silent deterioration.

quiz.q: You recheck a 58-year-old in the lobby. He is slumped, damp with sweat, heart rate 128 up from 96, and manual pressure 86/50. The triage nurse is mid-assessment with another patient. What do you do?
choices: Chart the numbers and wait until she finishes
Interrupt her or the charge nurse immediately with a structured report
Recheck in 10 minutes to confirm the trend
Move him to a quieter chair and monitor him yourself
quiz.why: Diaphoresis, rising heart rate, and hypotension together mean shock, which is minutes-critical. Interrupting is correct and expected. Charting, waiting for a confirming trend, or self-monitoring all delay the only action that helps.

quiz.q: Which waiting room observation is most concerning?
choices: A patient asking loudly how much longer the wait will be
A patient pacing near the door
A previously loud, demanding patient who is now silent with his eyes closed
A patient texting on his phone
quiz.why: Complaining requires energy, so a loud patient who becomes quiet has usually decompensated rather than settled. Demanding, pacing, and texting patients are, by themselves, signs of preserved effort and awareness.

quiz.q: A 2-year-old is pale and mottled, will not make eye contact, and has retractions. Heart rate 172, blood pressure 96/60, SpO2 93 percent. How should this be triaged?
choices: Low acuity, since the blood pressure is normal for age
High acuity: two sides of the pediatric assessment triangle are abnormal despite a normal blood pressure
Moderate acuity pending a fever check
Low acuity, since SpO2 is above 92 percent
quiz.why: Abnormal appearance and abnormal work of breathing plus abnormal skin circulation describe a sick child. Children maintain blood pressure until they are nearly decompensated, so a normal pressure is the least reassuring number on the list.

quiz.q: A 22-day-old infant has a rectal temperature of 38.1 C, is feeding well, and looks comfortable. What is the correct minimum acuity?
choices: ESI 5
ESI 4
ESI 3
ESI 2
quiz.why: Under 28 days of age, a temperature of 38.0 C or higher is a minimum ESI 2 requiring a full sepsis workup, because neonates cannot localize infection and may look well while bacteremic. Appearance and feeding do not lower this threshold.

quiz.q: A patient on a psychiatric hold is placed in a safe room and a sitter is assigned. Which additional step is required?
choices: Search and secure belongings and clothing, change into paper scrubs, and remove all ligature risks
Nothing further, since a sitter is present
Leave one personal item for comfort
Keep her phone charger so she can contact family
quiz.why: Safe rooms work by removing means as well as providing observation. Belongings routinely contain pills, blades, lighters, and cords, and a charger is a ligature risk. A sitter reduces but does not replace environmental control.

quiz.q: During a mass casualty incident using START, a patient is not breathing. You open the airway and he begins breathing at 12 per minute. What category?
choices: Black, expectant, since he required an intervention
Red, immediate, because he only breathes with a positioned airway
Yellow, delayed, since he is now breathing adequately
Green, minor, since his rate is normal
quiz.why: A patient who breathes only after an airway maneuver is immediate, red. Black is reserved for those who do not breathe after that maneuver. A normal rate obtained only through intervention does not make him delayed, and green is for the walking wounded.

quiz.q: A patient well known to the department for weekly visits arrives again with abdominal pain. What is the safest approach?
choices: Assume it is the usual complaint and assign a low acuity
Wait for the provider who knows him to assign the level
Triage this visit as a new visit, with a full set of vitals and no assumptions from prior visits
Assign a higher acuity automatically because of his visit frequency
quiz.why: Frequent visitors are a documented undertriage group precisely because familiarity replaces assessment. The correction is process: the same vitals and the same questions every visit. Automatic upgrades are equally unprincipled and waste resources.

quiz.q: Which statement about mass casualty triage is correct?
choices: It gives the most resources to the single sickest patient, as in daily practice
It aims for the greatest good for the greatest number, which can mean categorizing some patients as expectant
It eliminates the use of colored categories
It applies only to injuries, never to illness
quiz.why: When demand overwhelms supply, priorities invert toward survivable patients and an expectant category exists. Daily triage does the opposite. Color categories are central to START, and surge triage applies to any overwhelming event.

quiz.q: A 45-year-old with schizophrenia reports abdominal pain and appears internally preoccupied. What error should you guard against?
choices: Overtriage from an unnecessary workup
Diagnostic overshadowing, attributing a physical complaint to the psychiatric diagnosis
Assuming he is uninsured
Assuming he cannot give a history at all
quiz.why: Diagnostic overshadowing is the documented tendency to attribute new physical symptoms to an existing psychiatric diagnosis. Patients with serious mental illness have higher rates of serious medical disease and shorter life expectancy, not lower risk.

scenarios.title: Six in the lobby
scenarios.intro:
It is 1830 on a Tuesday. You are working triage with an experienced nurse. The department is full, with four boarders, and the charge nurse has two open beds. Six people arrive within about ten minutes and are sitting in the triage area.

1. A 46-year-old man, sweating, hand on his chest, says the pressure started forty minutes ago while he was eating.
2. A 19-year-old woman with a sore throat for two days, drinking a soda, no trouble breathing, temperature `37.9 C`.
3. A 71-year-old woman brought by her son, who says she has been 'not making sense' since about noon.
4. A 33-year-old man who twisted his ankle playing basketball, hopping, no deformity.
5. A 3-week-old infant whose mother reports a rectal temperature of `38.2 C` at home. The baby is feeding and looks comfortable.
6. A 58-year-old woman with two days of vomiting, heart rate `118`, SpO2 `91 percent` on room air.

The nurse is going to assign levels. You are going to make it possible.

steps.prompt: Before any levels are assigned, what is your single highest-value action?

choices.text: Get a 12-lead EKG on the 46-year-old with chest pressure, immediately
choices.feedback: Correct. The 10-minute door-to-EKG clock is already running and a STEMI is the only thing here that gets worse by the minute in a way you can change right now.

choices.text: Take full vitals on all six in arrival order
choices.feedback: Thorough, but arrival order is the one thing triage explicitly does not use. The chest pain needs the EKG before anyone gets a complete set.

choices.text: Get the infant's weight and temperature first
choices.feedback: The infant is genuinely high acuity and will need an accurate rectal temperature and a weight in kilograms. But the EKG has a hard 10-minute clock and takes four minutes. Do it first, then the baby.

choices.text: Start with the vomiting patient because her SpO2 is 91 percent
choices.feedback: Her danger-zone vitals are real and she will be upgraded. But she is not on a 10-minute clock, and an undiagnosed STEMI is.

steps.prompt: The EKG is done at minute 6 and handed to the physician, who takes the patient straight back. Five left, two open beds. Which two patients should occupy the nurse's attention next?

choices.text: The 71-year-old with new confusion and the 3-week-old with fever
choices.feedback: Right. New confusion is an independent ESI 2 gate, and fever under 28 days is a minimum ESI 2 with a full sepsis workup regardless of appearance. Both are quiet, well-looking, high-risk patients.

choices.text: The sore throat and the ankle, because they can be dispositioned fast and free up flow
choices.feedback: This is 'quick wins' thinking, and it is how ESI 2 patients end up in lobbies. Flow never outranks danger.

choices.text: The 58-year-old with vomiting and the ankle injury
choices.feedback: The vomiting patient belongs in the top group, but the ankle does not. You are pairing a correct choice with a low-acuity one.

choices.text: The 71-year-old with confusion and the 33-year-old with the ankle
choices.feedback: Half right. The confused patient is correct. A well-looking febrile neonate outranks an ankle by an enormous margin.

steps.prompt: The nurse asks you for the numbers she needs to finish the levels. Walk through what you obtain for the 58-year-old with vomiting, heart rate 118 and SpO2 91 percent.

choices.text: Recheck the SpO2 with a good waveform on a warm finger, recount respirations for a full 30 seconds, and verify the blood pressure manually
choices.feedback: Exactly. Two of her three danger-zone values sit right at the threshold, so the level depends on whether your numbers are real. Verify before the nurse upgrades or does not.

choices.text: Report the machine numbers as they are so the nurse can decide quickly
choices.feedback: Speed matters, but an unverified SpO2 of 91 percent could be a cold finger or could be real hypoxia. The whole level turns on this number.

choices.text: Put her on oxygen since her saturation is under 92 percent
choices.feedback: Out of scope. Oxygen is a medication and the rate is a dose. Report the number, get the nurse, and let them order it.

choices.text: Document the vitals and move on to the sore throat to keep the line moving
choices.feedback: Three abnormal values in one patient is not a line-moving moment. She meets danger-zone criteria in two categories.

steps.prompt: Verified: SpO2 `90 percent` on a good waveform, respiratory rate `26` counted, manual pressure `98/58`. The nurse upgrades her to ESI 2. That leaves the sore throat and the ankle. Assign them.

choices.text: Sore throat ESI 5, ankle ESI 4
choices.feedback: Correct. A rapid strep is point-of-care and a prescription is not a resource, so the sore throat counts zero. The ankle needs one X-ray; splints and crutches do not count.

choices.text: Both ESI 4
choices.feedback: The ankle is right. The sore throat counts zero resources because point-of-care swabs and prescriptions do not count, making it a 5.

choices.text: Both ESI 3, since both will need testing
choices.feedback: This is the classic inflation error. Counting point-of-care tests, splints, and prescriptions as resources pushes everyone to 3 and makes the scale meaningless.

choices.text: Sore throat ESI 4, ankle ESI 5
choices.feedback: Reversed. The X-ray is the resource; the throat swab is not.

steps.prompt: Final levels: chest pain went back, ESI 2. Confusion ESI 2. Neonate ESI 2. Vomiting ESI 2. Sore throat ESI 5, ankle ESI 4. Two beds, four ESI 2 patients. The sore throat and ankle will be waiting a while. What do you do for the lobby?

choices.text: Set recheck intervals: the ESI 2 patients get continuous or 15-minute checks until they are roomed, and the 4 and 5 get vitals every 60 to 120 minutes, and tell each patient honestly where they stand
choices.feedback: This is the whole job. Levels are snapshots; the recheck schedule is the safety net, and honest expectation setting prevents patients from leaving without being seen.

choices.text: Tell the sore throat and ankle they are next so they do not leave
choices.feedback: Never promise a position you do not control. With four ESI 2 patients ahead, they are not next, and being caught in it destroys trust.

choices.text: Focus on the ESI 2 patients only; the 4 and 5 are stable by definition
choices.feedback: ESI 4 and 5 predict resource use, not safety, and they are the least watched patients in the department. They still need scheduled rechecks.

choices.text: Ask the charge nurse whether a hallway bed or a boarder can be moved to make space for the ESI 2 patients
choices.feedback: Good flow thinking and worth saying. Just do not let it replace the reassessment schedule, which is the part you personally own.

scenarios.debrief:
Six patients, and only two of them looked sick. That is the lesson.

The chest pain announced itself, but the three quietest patients in the room, a confused elderly woman, a comfortable febrile newborn, and a woman who had been vomiting for two days, were all ESI 2. Each reached that level by a different route: new altered mental status as its own gate, a high-risk age-and-fever rule, and danger-zone vital signs upgrading a resource count.

The tech's contribution was not the level assignment. It was the 10-minute EKG, the verified SpO2 and manual blood pressure that decided whether the vomiting patient was a 3 or a 2, the accurate rectal temperature and kilogram weight on the infant, and the reassessment schedule for the people left in the chairs.

And notice the two errors you avoided: counting point-of-care tests and crutches as resources, which inflates everyone to ESI 3, and optimizing for quick discharges to improve flow, which is how a high-risk patient ends up waiting.

scenarios.title: She was a 3 an hour ago
scenarios.intro:
1640. Mrs. Adeyemi, 67, arrived at 1530 with two days of lower abdominal pain and decreased appetite. Triage assigned her ESI 3: labs and a CT expected, vitals unremarkable at heart rate `92`, blood pressure `138/78`, respiratory rate `18`, temperature `37.6 C`, SpO2 `97 percent`, pain `6/10`.

The department has no open beds. She has been in the waiting room for seventy minutes. You are doing the round of scheduled rechecks.

When you call her name, her daughter answers for her and says, "She's been kind of out of it the last twenty minutes."

steps.prompt: The daughter's sentence is the first piece of new information. What do you do with it?

choices.text: Treat it as a reported change in mental status and assess her right now, in the chair if needed
choices.feedback: Correct. Family are comparing against a baseline you have never seen, and new altered mental status is an independent ESI 2 gate. Their report is data.

choices.text: Note it and take the vitals in your normal order of rooms
choices.feedback: You will get there, but 'out of it' in a 67-year-old with abdominal pain is a sepsis and shock signal. This one jumps the queue of your rechecks.

choices.text: Reassure the daughter that waiting is tiring and people often get drowsy
choices.feedback: Plausible-sounding and dangerous. Explaining away a reported mental status change is a documented path to a lobby death.

choices.text: Ask the daughter to let you know if it gets worse
choices.feedback: You handed the monitoring job to a family member. The reassessment is yours.

steps.prompt: You bring her to the triage bay. She opens her eyes when you say her name but answers slowly and gets the month wrong. Her forehead is damp. Her skin is warm at the chest and cool at the fingertips.

choices.text: Verify the blood pressure manually, recount the respirations, and confirm the temperature route, then escalate
choices.feedback: Right instinct, and the verification takes ninety seconds. Just make sure escalation happens immediately after, not after a third recheck.

choices.text: Escalate immediately to the triage or charge nurse, and verify the manual pressure while you wait for them
choices.feedback: Best answer. This picture is sepsis with hypoperfusion, and verification and escalation should happen in parallel rather than in sequence.

choices.text: Recheck everything in 15 minutes to establish a trend before bothering anyone
choices.feedback: You already have the trend: heart rate 92 to 118, pressure 138 to 96, respirations 18 to 26, temperature 37.6 to 38.6, plus new confusion. That is the deterioration, not a hint of one.

choices.text: Give her water and a blanket, then recheck
choices.feedback: Nothing by mouth without a nurse's okay, especially in a patient who may go to surgery or who has an altered mental status and aspiration risk.

steps.prompt: You have the nurse's attention for about fifteen seconds. Say it.

choices.text: 'Mrs. Adeyemi in chair 6 doesn't look good, can you come see her?'
choices.feedback: It will get the nurse moving, which is better than nothing. But she arrives with no information and has to start from zero.

choices.text: 'Chair 6, Mrs. Adeyemi, ESI 3 abdominal pain since 1530. She's newly confused per her daughter, diaphoretic, cool fingers. Heart rate 92 to 118, pressure 138 over 78 down to 96 over 52 verified manually, respirations 26, temp 38.6, sat 93. I think she needs to come back now.'
choices.feedback: This is the report. Who, what changed with the before and after numbers, what you did, and what you need. The nurse can act on this without asking you anything.

choices.text: 'Her pressure is 96 over 52.'
choices.feedback: One number out of context. A pressure of 96 over 52 in isolation could be someone's baseline. The change from 138 over 78 is the whole story.

choices.text: 'I think she's septic, she needs a lactate and blood cultures.'
choices.feedback: Your pattern recognition may well be right, and that instinct is worth having. But stating a diagnosis and ordering the workup is outside your role. Report the findings; the diagnosis is theirs.

steps.prompt: The nurse upgrades her to ESI 2, the charge nurse pulls a boarder into the hallway to free a monitored bed, and a code sepsis is called. The team is converging. What do you do in the next five minutes?

choices.text: Draw the lactate and two sets of blood cultures with sterile technique before antibiotics, apply the monitor, and get a full repeat set of vitals
choices.feedback: This is precisely the tech's contribution to the 1-hour bundle. Cultures before antibiotics is the step only you can protect.

choices.text: Start the 30 mL/kg fluid bolus
choices.feedback: Out of scope. Hanging and titrating fluids is a nursing task. You can set up the line, get the pump, and have the bag ready.

choices.text: Wait for specific instructions so you do not get in the way
choices.feedback: In a called alert, the tasks are known. Standing by during a sepsis alert wastes the minutes the bundle is measured in.

choices.text: Get her to CT right away since an abdominal source is likely
choices.feedback: The CT is coming, but not before cultures, antibiotics, and fluids are underway, and not before she is stable enough to leave the department.

steps.prompt: Antibiotics are in at 1704, twenty-four minutes after you first spoke to her daughter. She is on fluids and being admitted. Her daughter finds you in the hallway and asks, 'Is my mother going to be okay? What is happening to her?'

choices.text: 'She has sepsis from an abdominal infection, but we caught it in time.'
choices.feedback: You do not deliver a diagnosis or a prognosis, and 'caught it in time' is a promise nobody can make. Both are out of scope.

choices.text: 'I can't speak to her diagnosis, but I can tell you exactly what we're doing: she's on antibiotics and fluids and continuous monitoring, and she's being admitted. Let me get her nurse to talk with you.'
choices.feedback: Right balance. Concrete facts about actions, no diagnosis, no prognosis, and a real path to the person who can answer. This is what families actually need.

choices.text: 'I'm not allowed to discuss that.'
choices.feedback: Accurate and cold. She is frightened and she was the person whose observation started all of this. Give her something true and a route to more.

choices.text: 'You did the right thing telling me she seemed off. Her nurse will come talk to you about what's going on, and I'll go get her now.'
choices.feedback: Also good, and worth saying. Families who are told their observations mattered report more, and reporting families catch deterioration.

scenarios.debrief:
An ESI level is a photograph, and this patient moved.

The change was announced by a family member, not a monitor. 'She's been kind of out of it' in a 67-year-old with abdominal pain is a sepsis presentation until proven otherwise, and new altered mental status is an independent ESI 2 gate on its own.

The pattern to keep: it was the delta, not the absolute values, that told the story. A pressure of `96/52` alone means little. A drop from `138/78` to `96/52` with a heart rate climbing from `92` to `118`, respirations from `18` to `26`, a temperature rising to `38.6 C`, cool fingertips with a warm chest, and new confusion is compensated shock heading toward decompensated. Any two of those together should move your feet.

Your actual contributions were narrow and decisive: you believed the family, you assessed instead of explaining the change away, you verified the abnormal numbers manually, you escalated with before-and-after values in one structured sentence, and you drew cultures before antibiotics. You never named a diagnosis, never ordered a test, never hung a fluid, and never made a promise about the outcome.
